Lesson 5 on founder growth: Treat QTs and comments as networking infrastructure ↓

Most founder content strategies over-focus on original posts and under-focus on replies.

For a growing founder account, QTs and comments are networking infrastructure.

✦ Original posts tell people what the founder thinks.
✦ Comments and QTs show how the founder thinks in context.

A founder should comment where the market is already paying attention, but with one rule: never comment just to be visible.

Good comments usually do one of four things:
- add data
- add lived experience
- add a missing caveat
- add a useful reframing

Weak comments usually do one of three things:
- agree without adding anything
- force a company mention
- try to sound smarter than the original post

QTs are especially useful when the founder can connect someone else’s observation to the company’s broader thesis.

But they shouldn’t become a lazy quote-tweet machine.
A QT needs a point of view strong enough to stand on its own.

Read the full story ↓
https://t.co/l4JiXSqVMo

Spent a few hours cancelling subscriptions this morning, ended up saving $5,877 a year so far.

I uploaded my credit card statements into Claude and had it organize every subscription into a spreadsheet.

Then used Claude Co-work to go through and actually help cancel them (or draft the email if they don’t have a cancel button). 

The apps fell into 3 buckets:

/1  Don't use it anymore

Sometimes I'd sign up for a free trial and forget to cancel. Other times I'd replace a tool and never cancel the old one.
Notion - was great a few years ago but don’t really use it anymore.
Gamma. Used it for slides, but I prefer Claude Design now.

/2 Free alternatives.
Asked Claude to find free or cheaper alternatives to the big names. Found quite a few:

• Loom → @cap
• Calendly → Cal com
• Wispr Flow → FluidVoice
• YNAB (personal budgeting) → Actual Budget

The value prop isn't just free. Some of the alternatives focus on privacy.
I didn't love the idea of everything I dictate running through Wispr Flow's servers when I can self host instead.

I bought a mac mini during the OpenClaw craze a while back, so it’s for me to self host a lot of stuff.

3. Vibecode your own.

For a lot of apps, you can just vibecode your own solution with Claude, Hermes, etc.

• Front com (email management) → vibecoded my own
• To do list → vibecoded my own

Replacing an entire app sounds like a pain in the ass, but you're not replacing the entire app. 

Hear me out.

Most of this software kept adding features I didn't want or need. I'd sign up for one simple tool, and they'd keep piling on bloat like "AI."

Why? Add features → raise the price.

So when I vibecode, everything gets stripped down to the bare essentials. The shit I actually signed up for and want to use. 

Caveat, don’t try to replace everything. Security risks or the maintenance involved can cost more than just paying for the software.

It's your hard earned money. Don't let it go to waste.

The value prop isn't just free. Some of the alternatives focus on privacy.
I didn't love the idea of everything I dictate running through Wispr Flow's servers when I can self host instead.

I bought a mac mini during the OpenClaw craze a while back, so it’s for me to self host a lot of stuff.

3. Vibecode your own.

For a lot of apps, you can just vibecode your own solution with Claude, Hermes, etc.

• Front com (email management) → vibecoded my own
• To do list → vibecoded my own

Replacing an entire app sounds like a pain in the ass, but you're not replacing the entire app. 

Hear me out.

Most of this software kept adding features I didn't want or need. I'd sign up for one simple tool, and they'd keep piling on bloat like "AI."

Why? Add features → raise the price.

So when I vibecode, everything gets stripped down to the bare essentials. The shit I actually signed up for and want to use. 

Caveat, don’t try to replace everything. Security risks or the maintenance involved can cost more than just paying for the software.

It's your hard earned money. Don't let it go to waste.

tweets.text:
We're now in a double exponential. The first real example of Reed's Law in history.

I've been building toward this idea for years. I first wrote about Reed's Law back in 2022, called AI the first true example of it in 2023, and by 2025 I was pointing out that almost nobody had priced what it actually means.

Quick version for anyone who hasn't gone down this hole:

Metcalfe's Law says a network's value grows with the square of its users… it's why the internet ate the world.

Reed's Law goes further: when the members can form groups, value scales with two to the power of the number of members. Vastly faster.

It's been true on paper for decades but never showed up cleanly in reality, because the nodes were humans, and humans are slow to form groups.

The nodes are no longer human. AI agents form and dissolve coalitions in milliseconds, a million at a time. For the first time the maths has something to run on with no friction.

That's what this chart is. On a log scale an exponential is a straight line. Look what happens after 2020...

Every previous technology wave gave us decades to adapt. This one gives us years.

Your job, your savings, the whole economy is about to change faster than any institution can keep up with.

You can't even picture a double exponential. Neither can I. That's the whole point.

Aug 6 Asia session (AM)

- Wild overnight vol in the US session - painful if you're asleep through it.
- Sticking with the semis dispersion view. Main reason I'm avoiding memory.
- SNDK: monster print, sold off anyway

- Revenue $8.97B vs ~$8.48B est (+51% QoQ, +372% YoY)
- Non-GAAP EPS $39.25 vs ~$34.96 est; GAAP $43.97
- Non-GAAP GM 84.6% (vs 78.4% prior Q, 26.4% YoY) ; insane for memory, pure NAND supply-tightness pricing power
- But Q1'27 guide $10.3–10.8B vs $11.16B Street → couldn't beat the guide

Why: rate of change > raw numbers

- Hyperscaler capex $1B → $100B = 10x (+$99B). $100B → $300B = 3x (+$200B). 

Bigger dollars, slower ROC → parabolas hit a ceiling.

The rotation 
- Semis (AMD, SNDK, SK Hynix) printing and selling off.
- Non-semis doing the opposite - SHOP guided higher, gapped up.

You don't get it, I'm not talking about not using the ATM, I'm recommending only hitting the ATM at their discretion in a range above $100, for example $100-$105, instead of hitting it automatically at $100.00

In the current situation, they are offering a free short at $100 and they are preventing the price from ever having an average value close to $100. 

Because they can't reduce the volatility to less than a 10% range, by capping all upside above $100 they'll get the 10% volatility anyway but it'll be from $90 to $100

I am pretty certain they will fold on this anyway at some point, just like Strive did, but by now it should be an obvious STRC improvement that anyone interested in MSTR for a while should see! I don't understand why it's not obvious for all the True North team
